And he was supposed to be so well-educated and clever. This is what a foreign education amounts to! I hope that no one in Moscow will receive him, no matter how rich he is. They tried to introduce him to me, but I flatly refused — I have daughters to think of."

"Why do you say he's rich?" asked the countess, turning away from the girls, who immediately put on expressions of elaborate disinterest. "All his children are illegitimate. I believe Pierre is illegitimate too."
The visitor made a dismissive gesture.
"I think there must be a good twenty of them."
Princess Anna Mikhaylovna joined the conversation, clearly wanting to display her connections and her insider knowledge of society.

"The fact of the matter is," she said meaningfully, also lowering her voice, "everyone knows Count Cyril's reputation. He's lost track of how many children he has. But this Pierre was always his favorite."
"How handsome the old man still was, just a year ago!" remarked the countess. "I've never seen a more handsome man."

"He's changed terribly now," said Anna Mikhaylovna. "Well, as I was saying — Prince Vasili is next in line to inherit through his wife, but the count is very fond of Pierre. He looked after his education and even wrote to the Emperor about him. So when he dies — and he's so ill now that it could happen at any moment; Doctor Lorrain has come specially from Petersburg — no one knows who will get his enormous fortune: Pierre or Prince Vasili. Forty thousand serfs and millions of rubles! I know all this firsthand — Prince Vasili told me himself. Besides, Cyril Vladimirovich is my mother's second cousin. He's also Boris's godfather," she added, as if this last detail were of no particular importance.
"Prince Vasili arrived in Moscow yesterday. I hear he's here on some official inspection," the visitor remarked.
"Yes, but between us," said the princess, "that's just a cover story. The real reason is that he's come to see Count Cyril Vladimirovich, having heard how ill he is."

"But you know, my dear, that was a marvelous joke," said the count. Noticing that the older visitor wasn't listening, he turned to the young ladies. "I can just picture the policeman — what a sight he must have been!"

And waving his arms to impersonate the policeman, his portly frame shook once more with deep, resonant laughter — the laughter of a man who always eats well and, especially, drinks well. "So you will come to dinner, won't you?" he said.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: The only young people left in the drawing room — not counting the young lady visitor and the countess's eldest daughter, who was four years older than her sister and already behaved like an adult — were Nicholas and Sonya, the niece. Sonya was a slender little brunette with tender eyes veiled by long lashes, thick black braids coiled twice around her head, and a warm tint to her complexion, especially visible in the color of her slender but graceful and muscular arms and neck. In the gracefulness of her movements, the softness and flexibility of her small limbs, and a certain shyness and reserve in her manner, she was like a pretty half-grown kitten that promises to become a beautiful cat. She clearly felt it was proper to show interest in the general conversation by smiling, but despite herself, her eyes — from beneath those thick long lashes — followed her cousin who was about to join the army with such passionate, girlish adoration that her smile couldn't fool anyone for a moment. It was obvious the kitten had settled down only to spring up with renewed energy and play with her cousin again, as soon as they too could escape the drawing room, like Natasha and Boris before them.

"Ah yes, my dear," said the count, turning to the visitor and gesturing toward Nicholas. "His friend Boris has become an officer, and so out of friendship he's leaving the university — and me, his old father — to join the army, my dear. And he had a position all lined up for him in the Archives Department! Now that's friendship for you," the count remarked in a questioning tone.
"But they say war has been declared," replied the visitor.
"They've been saying that for ages," said the count, "and they'll say it again and again, and that'll be the end of it. My dear, that's friendship for you," he repeated. "He's joining the hussars."
The visitor, not knowing what to say, shook her head.

"It's got nothing to do with friendship," Nicholas burst out, flaring up and turning away as though from a shameful accusation. "It's not about friendship at all. I simply feel the army is my calling."
He glanced at his cousin and the young lady visitor; both were looking at him with approving smiles.

"Colonel Schubert of the Pavlograd Hussars is dining with us today. He's been here on leave and is taking Nicholas back with him. What can you do?" said the count, shrugging his shoulders and speaking lightly about a matter that clearly upset him.

"I've already told you, Papa," said his son, "that if you don't want to let me go, I'll stay. But I know I'm no good anywhere except in the army. I'm not a diplomat or a government clerk — I don't know how to hide what I feel." As he said this, he kept glancing with a young man's flirtatiousness at Sonya and the young lady visitor.
The little kitten, feasting her eyes on him, looked ready at any moment to spring into action and reveal her playful nature.

"All right, all right!" said the old count. "He always gets so heated! This Bonaparte has turned all their heads. They all dream of how he rose from a junior officer to become Emperor. Well, well — God willing," he added, not noticing his visitor's sarcastic smile.
The adults began talking about Bonaparte. Julie Karagina turned to young Rostov.
"What a shame you weren't at the Arkharovs' on Thursday. It was so dull without you," she said, giving him a tender smile.

The young man, flattered, moved closer to her with a flirtatious smile and drew the smiling Julie into a private conversation, completely unaware that his casual charm had stabbed Sonya's heart. She blushed and smiled unnaturally. In the middle of his talk, he glanced over at her. She shot him a look of passionate anger, and barely managing to hold back her tears while keeping up the forced smile on her lips, she stood and left the room. All of Nicholas's good spirits vanished. He waited for the first pause in conversation, then left the room with a troubled face to find Sonya.

"How plainly all these young people wear their hearts on their sleeves!" said Anna Mikhaylovna, gesturing toward Nicholas as he left. "[Speaking in French] Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood," she added.
The original French footnote: Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood.

"Yes," said the countess when the brightness the young people had brought to the room had faded, and as if answering a question no one had asked but which was always on her mind, "and how much suffering, how much worry one goes through so that we can take joy in them now! And yet the worry now is even greater than the joy. One is always, always anxious! Especially at this age — so perilous for both girls and boys."
"It all depends on the upbringing," the visitor remarked.

"Yes, quite right," the countess went on. "Until now I have always, thank God, been my children's friend and had their full confidence" — she said this repeating the mistake so many parents make who believe their children have no secrets from them. "I know I will always be my daughters' closest confidante, and that even if Nicholas, with his impulsive nature, does get into some trouble — boys can't help it — he'll never turn out like those Petersburg young men."

"Yes, they're wonderful, wonderful children," the count chimed in — he always resolved questions that seemed difficult by declaring everything to be wonderful. "Just imagine — wants to be a hussar! What's a father to do, my dear?"
"What a charming creature your younger daughter is," said the visitor. "A little volcano!"

"Yes, a real volcano," agreed the count. "Takes after me! And what a voice she has! Though she's my daughter, I'll say it honestly — she'll be a singer, a second Salomoni! We've hired an Italian to give her lessons."
"Isn't she too young? I've heard it can damage the voice to train it at that age."
"Oh, not at all too young!" replied the count. "Why, our mothers were getting married at twelve or thirteen."

"And she's already in love with Boris. Can you imagine!" said the countess with a gentle smile, looking at Boris. She continued, clearly preoccupied with a thought that always occupied her: "You see, if I were strict with her and forbade it... who knows what they might get up to behind my back" — she meant that they would be kissing — "but as things stand, I know every word she says. She comes running to me on her own every evening and tells me everything. Maybe I spoil her, but really it seems like the best approach. I was stricter with her older sister."
"Yes, I was brought up quite differently," remarked the good-looking eldest daughter, Countess Vera, with a smile.

But the smile did nothing to enhance Vera's beauty, as smiles usually do. On the contrary, it gave her an unnatural and therefore unpleasant expression. Vera was attractive, not at all stupid, quick at learning, well brought up, and had a pleasant voice. What she said was true and fitting. And yet, oddly enough, everyone — the visitors and the countess alike — looked at her as if wondering why she had said it, and they all felt uncomfortable.
"People always try too hard with their eldest children and attempt to make something exceptional of them," said the visitor.
"No use denying it, my dear — the countess was too ambitious with Vera," said the count. "Well, what of it? She's turned out wonderfully all the same," he added with a wink at Vera.
The guests rose and said their goodbyes, promising to return for dinner.
"What manners! I thought they'd never leave," said the countess after seeing her guests out.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: When Natasha ran out of the drawing room, she only went as far as the conservatory. There she stopped and stood listening to the conversation in the drawing room, waiting for Boris to come out. She was already growing impatient and stamped her foot, on the verge of tears because he wasn't coming quickly enough, when she heard the young man's measured steps approaching — neither fast nor slow. At this, Natasha darted among the flower tubs and hid.

Boris paused in the middle of the room, looked around, brushed a speck of dust from his uniform sleeve, and walked up to a mirror to examine his handsome face. Natasha, perfectly still, peered out from her hiding place to see what he would do. He stood before the mirror for a moment, smiled, and walked toward the other door. Natasha was about to call out to him but changed her mind. "Let him look for me," she thought. No sooner had Boris left than Sonya burst in through the other door — flushed, tearful, muttering angrily. Natasha suppressed her first impulse to run out to her and stayed hidden, watching — as if wearing an invisible cloak — to see what would unfold. She was experiencing a strange new pleasure. Sonya, still muttering, kept glancing toward the drawing room door. It opened and Nicholas came in.
"Sonya, what's wrong? How can you?" he said, hurrying up to her.
"It's nothing, nothing — leave me alone!" Sonya sobbed.
"I know what this is about."
"Well, if you know, then go back to her!"
"So-o-onya! How can you torment me and yourself like this over nothing?" said Nicholas, taking her hand.
Sonya didn't pull it away and stopped crying. Natasha, not moving, barely breathing, watched from her hiding spot with shining eyes. "What will happen now?" she wondered.
"Sonya! What does anyone else in the world mean to me? You — you alone are everything!" said Nicholas. "And I'll prove it to you."
"I don't like you talking like that."
"All right, I won't. Just forgive me, Sonya!" He drew her close and kissed her.
"Oh, how lovely," thought Natasha. And when Sonya and Nicholas had left the conservatory, she slipped out and called Boris to her.
"Boris, come here," she said with a sly, meaningful look. "I have something to tell you. Here, over here!" And she led him into the conservatory, to the spot among the tubs where she had been hiding.
Boris followed her, smiling.
"What's the something?" he asked.
She grew flustered, looked around, and spotting the doll she had tossed onto one of the tubs, picked it up.
"Kiss the doll," she said.
Boris studied her eager face attentively and kindly but said nothing.
"You don't want to? Well then, come here," she said, moving deeper among the plants and tossing the doll aside. "Closer, closer!" she whispered.
She grabbed the young officer by his cuffs, and a look of gravity and fear appeared on her flushed face.
"And me? Would you like to kiss me?" she whispered, almost inaudibly, looking up at him from under her brows, smiling and nearly crying with excitement.
Boris blushed.
"You're so funny!" he said, leaning down toward her and blushing even deeper. But he hesitated and did nothing.
Suddenly she sprang up onto a tub to be taller than him, threw both her slender bare arms around his neck, tossed back her hair, and kissed him full on the lips.
Then she slipped down among the flowerpots on the other side of the tubs and stood with her head bowed.
"Natasha," he said, "you know that I love you, but..."
"You're in love with me?" Natasha interrupted.
"Yes, I am, but please — let's not do things like that.... In another four years... then I'll ask for your hand."
Natasha thought it over.
"Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen," she counted on her slender little fingers. "All right! So it's settled?"
A smile of joy and satisfaction lit up her eager face.
"Settled!" Boris replied.
"Forever?" said the little girl. "Until death itself?"
She took his arm and, beaming with happiness, walked with him into the next room.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: After receiving her visitors, the countess was so tired that she gave orders to let no one else in, but told the doorman to make sure to invite anyone who came "to offer congratulations" to stay for dinner. The countess wanted a private conversation with her childhood friend, Princess Anna Mikhaylovna, whom she hadn't properly seen since her return from Petersburg. Anna Mikhaylovna, with her care-worn but pleasant face, pulled her chair closer to the countess's.
"I'll be completely honest with you," said Anna Mikhaylovna. "There aren't many of us old friends left! That's why I value your friendship so much."
Anna Mikhaylovna glanced at Vera and paused. The countess squeezed her friend's hand.
"Vera," she said to her eldest daughter, who was clearly not a favorite, "how can you have so little tact? Can't you see you're not wanted here? Go join the other girls, or..."
The beautiful Vera smiled contemptuously but didn't seem at all hurt.
"If you'd told me sooner, Mama, I would have left," she replied, and rose to go to her room.

But as she passed through the sitting room, she noticed two couples seated at the windows, one pair at each. She stopped and smiled scornfully. Sonya sat close to Nicholas, who was copying out verses for her — the first he had ever written. Boris and Natasha were at the other window and fell silent when Vera came in. Sonya and Natasha looked at Vera with guilty, happy faces.
It was a sweet, touching sight — these girls in love. But clearly the scene stirred no pleasant feelings in Vera.
"How many times have I asked you not to take my things?" she said. "You have your own room." And she took the inkstand from Nicholas.
"Just a minute, just a minute," he said, dipping his pen.
"You always manage to do things at the worst possible time," Vera went on. "You came bursting into the drawing room in a way that made everyone embarrassed for you."
Though what she said was perfectly fair, perhaps for that very reason no one replied, and the four just looked at one another. She lingered in the room with the inkstand in her hand.
"And at your age, what secrets can there be between Natasha and Boris, or between you two? It's all nonsense!"
"Come on, Vera, what does it matter to you?" said Natasha in her defense, speaking very gently.
She seemed that day to be kinder and more affectionate to everyone than usual.
"How silly," said Vera. "I'm embarrassed for you. Secrets, really!"
"Everyone has their own secrets," Natasha replied, growing heated. "We don't meddle in your business with Berg."
"I should hope not," said Vera, "because there could never be anything improper in my behavior. But I will tell Mama how you're carrying on with Boris."
"Natalya Ilyinichna has been perfectly proper with me," Boris remarked. "I have nothing to complain about."

"Oh, don't, Boris! You're such a diplomat, it's really tiresome," said Natasha in a wounded voice that trembled slightly. (She used the word 'diplomat,' which was very fashionable among the children just then, in their own special sense.) "Why does she have to bother me?" And turning to Vera she said: "You'll never understand it, because you've never loved anyone. You have no heart! You're a Madame de Genlis and nothing more" — this nickname, given to Vera by Nicholas, was considered a devastating insult — "and your greatest pleasure is being unpleasant to people! Go flirt with Berg as much as you want," she finished quickly.
"At least I don't chase after young men in front of guests..."
"Well, you've done what you came to do," Nicholas cut in. "You've said something unpleasant to everyone and upset them. Let's go to the nursery."
All four of them, like a flock of startled birds, got up and left the room.
"The unpleasant things were said to me," Vera remarked. "I said nothing unpleasant to anyone."
"Madame de Genlis! Madame de Genlis!" laughing voices shouted through the door.

The beautiful Vera, who had such an irritating and unpleasant effect on everyone, smiled and, apparently unmoved by what had been said to her, went to the mirror to adjust her hair and scarf. Looking at her own handsome face, she seemed to grow even colder and calmer.
In the drawing room, the conversation was still going on.

"Ah, my dear," said the countess, "my life is no bed of roses either. Don't I know that at the rate we're spending, our money won't last long? It's all because of the Club and his easy-going ways. Even in the country we get no peace — theatricals, hunting, and heaven knows what else! But let's not talk about me. Tell me how you manage everything. I'm always amazed at you, Annette — how at your age you can rush off alone by carriage to Moscow, to Petersburg, to all those ministers and important people, and deal with them all! It's truly remarkable. How did you get things settled? I could never do it."

"Ah, my love," replied Anna Mikhaylovna, "God grant you never know what it's like to be left a widow without money, with a son you love to distraction! You learn a great deal then," she added with a certain pride. "That lawsuit taught me so much. When I need to see one of those important people, I write a note: 'Princess So-and-So requests an interview with So-and-So,' and then I take a cab and go myself — two, three, four times if necessary — until I get what I want. I don't care what anyone thinks of me."

"And who did you approach about Boris?" asked the countess. "Your boy is already an officer in the Guards, while my Nicholas is going in as a cadet. There's no one to put in a word for him. Who did you go to?"

"To Prince Vasili. He was so kind. He agreed to everything right away and presented the matter to the Emperor," said Princess Anna Mikhaylovna enthusiastically, completely forgetting all the humiliation she had endured to achieve her goal.

"Has Prince Vasili aged much?" asked the countess. "I haven't seen him since we performed together in the Rumyantsovs' theatricals. I expect he's forgotten me. He used to pay me attention in those days," the countess said with a smile.

"He's exactly the same as ever," replied Anna Mikhaylovna, "overflowing with charm. His position hasn't gone to his head at all. He said to me, 'I'm sorry I can do so little for you, dear Princess. I'm at your disposal.' Yes, he's a fine man and a very kind relative. But, Nataly, you know how I love my son — I would do anything for his happiness! And my affairs are in such a bad state that my situation is truly desperate," Anna Mikhaylovna went on sadly, lowering her voice. "My wretched lawsuit eats up everything I have and gets nowhere. Would you believe it — I literally don't have a penny and have no idea how to outfit Boris for the army." She took out her handkerchief and began to cry. "I need five hundred rubles, and all I have is a single twenty-five-ruble note. I'm in such a state... My only hope now is Count Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov. If he won't help his own godson — you know he's Boris's godfather — and give him something for his upkeep, all my efforts will have been for nothing... I won't be able to equip him."
The countess's eyes filled with tears and she sat in thoughtful silence.

"I often think — though perhaps it's a sin," said the princess, "that here is Count Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov, so rich, all alone... that enormous fortune... and what is his life worth? It's a burden to him, while Boris's life is only just beginning..."
"Surely he'll leave something to Boris," said the countess.

"Heaven only knows, my dear! These rich grandees are so selfish. Still, I'm going to take Boris and go see him right now. I'll speak to him directly. Let people think what they will — it's all the same to me when my son's future is at stake." The princess stood up. "It's two o'clock now and you dine at four. There's just enough time."
And like the practical Petersburg woman she was, who knew how to make the most of every hour, Anna Mikhaylovna sent for her son and went out to the anteroom with him.
"Goodbye, my dear," she said to the countess at the door, then added in a whisper so her son wouldn't hear: "Wish me luck."

"Are you going to Count Kirill Vladimirovich, my dear?" asked the count, coming out of the dining room into the anteroom. "If he's feeling better, do ask Pierre to come to dinner. He's been to our house before, you know — he danced with the children. Be sure to invite him, my dear. We'll see how our cook Taras outdoes himself today. He claims Count Orlov never gave a dinner as fine as ours will be!"

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Pierre, as it turned out, had never managed to settle on a career in Petersburg and had been expelled from the city for disorderly behavior and sent to Moscow. The story people told about him at Count Rostov's was true—Pierre really had helped tie a policeman to a bear. He had now been in Moscow for several days, staying as usual at his father's house. Although he expected the story of his escapade to have already reached Moscow and assumed that the ladies living with his father—who had never liked him—would have used it to turn the count against him, he nevertheless went to his father's part of the house on the day he arrived. Entering the drawing room where the princesses spent most of their time, he greeted the ladies, two of whom were sitting at embroidery frames while a third read aloud. It was the eldest who was reading—the one who had met Anna Mikhaylovna. The two younger ones were embroidering: both were rosy and pretty, differing only in that one had a small mole on her lip that made her much prettier. Pierre was received as though he were a corpse or a leper. The eldest princess paused in her reading and silently stared at him with frightened eyes; the second adopted exactly the same expression; while the youngest, the one with the mole, who had a cheerful and lively nature, bent over her frame to hide a smile at the amusing scene she saw coming. She pulled her wool down through the canvas and, barely able to keep from laughing, stooped as if trying to make out the pattern.
"How do you do, cousin?" said Pierre. "You don't recognize me?"
"I recognize you only too well. Too well."
"How is the count? Can I see him?" asked Pierre, awkward as usual, but not embarrassed.
"The count is suffering physically and mentally, and it seems you've done your best to add to his mental suffering."
"Can I see the count?" Pierre asked again.

"Hmm... If you want to kill him—kill him outright—then go ahead and see him. Olga, go check whether Uncle's broth is ready. It's almost time," she added, making it clear to Pierre that they were busy, busy taking care of his father—while he, Pierre, was apparently busy only causing the old man grief.
Olga left. Pierre stood looking at the sisters, then bowed and said, "Then I'll go to my rooms. You'll let me know when I can see him."
He left the room, followed by the low but clear laughter of the sister with the mole.

The next day Prince Vasili arrived and settled into the count's house. He sent for Pierre and said, "My dear fellow, if you behave here the way you did in Petersburg, you'll come to a very bad end. That's all I have to say to you. The count is very, very ill, and you must not see him at all."
Since then Pierre had not been disturbed and had spent all his time in his rooms upstairs.

When Boris appeared at his door, Pierre was pacing up and down his room, stopping now and then at a corner to make threatening gestures at the wall as if running an invisible enemy through with a sword, glaring savagely over his spectacles, then resuming his walk, muttering inaudible words, shrugging his shoulders, and waving his arms.

"England is finished," he declared, scowling and pointing his finger at an unseen someone. "Mr. Pitt, as a traitor to the nation and to the rights of man, is sentenced to..." But before Pierre—who at that moment was imagining himself to be Napoleon, having just pulled off the dangerous crossing of the English Channel and captured London—could pronounce Pitt's sentence, he noticed a well-built, handsome young officer entering his room. Pierre stopped. He had left Moscow when Boris was a boy of fourteen and had completely forgotten him, but in his usual impulsive and warm-hearted way, he grabbed Boris's hand with a friendly smile.
"Do you remember me?" asked Boris quietly, with a pleasant smile. "I've come with my mother to see the count, but it seems he isn't well."
"Yes, he seems to be ill. People keep disturbing him," Pierre answered, trying to remember who this young man was.
Boris could tell that Pierre didn't recognize him but didn't feel the need to introduce himself and, without the slightest embarrassment, looked Pierre straight in the face.
"Count Rostov invites you to dinner today," he said, after a lengthy pause that made Pierre uncomfortable.

"Ah, Count Rostov!" Pierre exclaimed happily. "Then you must be his son Ilya? Just think, I didn't recognize you at first. Do you remember how we went to Sparrow Hills with Madame Jacquot? That was ages ago..."

"You're mistaken," said Boris calmly, with a bold and faintly sarcastic smile. "I'm Boris, son of Princess Anna Mikhaylovna Drubetskaya. Rostov the father is Ilya, and his son is Nicholas. I never knew any Madame Jacquot."
Pierre waved his head and arms as though swatting away mosquitoes.

"Oh dear, what am I saying? I've gotten everything mixed up. There are so many relatives in Moscow! So you're Boris? Of course. Well, now we know where we stand. And what do you think of the Boulogne expedition? The English will come out badly, you know, if Napoleon gets across the Channel. I think the expedition is perfectly feasible. If only Villeneuve doesn't make a mess of things!"
Boris knew nothing about the Boulogne expedition; he didn't read the papers, and this was the first time he'd heard Villeneuve's name.

"We here in Moscow are more occupied with dinner parties and gossip than with politics," he said in his quiet, ironic way. "I don't know anything about it and haven't thought about it. Moscow is mainly busy with gossip," he continued. "Right now everyone's talking about you and your father."
Pierre smiled in his good-natured way, as if worried that his companion might say something he'd later regret. But Boris spoke clearly, precisely, and drily, looking Pierre straight in the eye.
"Moscow has nothing better to do than gossip," Boris went on. "Everyone is wondering who the count will leave his fortune to, though he may well outlive us all, which I sincerely hope he does..."
"Yes, it's all very horrible," Pierre broke in. "Very horrible."
Pierre was still afraid this officer might accidentally say something embarrassing.
"And it must seem to you," said Boris, flushing slightly but not changing his tone or manner, "it must seem to you that everyone is trying to get something from the rich man."
"That's exactly what it seems like," Pierre thought.

"But I just want to say, to avoid any misunderstanding, that you're quite wrong if you count me or my mother among such people. We are very poor, but for my own part—precisely because your father is rich—I don't consider myself a relative of his, and neither I nor my mother would ever ask or accept anything from him."

For a long time Pierre couldn't take in what Boris was saying, but when he did, he jumped up from the sofa, grabbed Boris by the elbow in his quick, clumsy way, and, blushing far more than Boris, began speaking with a mixture of shame and frustration.
"Wait, this is strange! Do you think that I... who would think...? I know perfectly well..."
But Boris cut him off again.

"I'm glad I've spoken my mind. Perhaps you didn't like it? You'll have to forgive me," he said, putting Pierre at ease rather than the other way around, "but I always make it a rule to speak frankly. So—what answer should I bring back? Will you come to dinner at the Rostovs'?"
And Boris, having apparently discharged an unpleasant duty, extricated himself from an awkward situation, and deposited someone else in it, became entirely pleasant again.

"No, but listen," said Pierre, calming down. "You're a wonderful fellow! What you just said was good—really good. Of course you don't know me. We haven't seen each other since we were children. You might have thought that I... I understand, I completely understand. I couldn't have done it myself—I wouldn't have had the nerve—but it's splendid. I'm very glad to know you. It's odd," he added after a pause, "that you'd suspect me!" He began to laugh. "Well, what of it! I hope we'll get to know each other better." And he squeezed Boris's hand. "You know, I haven't been in to see the count once. He hasn't sent for me... I feel sorry for him as a human being, but what can you do?"
"So you think Napoleon will actually manage to get an army across?" asked Boris with a smile.
Pierre saw that Boris wanted to change the subject, and since he felt the same way, he launched into the advantages and disadvantages of the Boulogne expedition.

A footman came in to fetch Boris—the princess was leaving. Pierre, wanting to get to know Boris better, promised to come to dinner, and warmly pressing his hand, looked affectionately at him over his spectacles. After Boris left, Pierre continued pacing up and down the room for a long time, no longer stabbing an imaginary enemy with his imaginary sword, but smiling at the memory of that pleasant, intelligent, and resolute young man.
As often happens in early youth, especially for someone who leads a lonely life, he felt an inexplicable warmth toward this young man and decided they would be friends.
Prince Vasili saw the princess off. She held a handkerchief to her eyes and her face was tearful.

"It's dreadful, dreadful!" she kept saying. "But whatever it costs me, I will do my duty. I'll come and spend the night. He must not be left like this. Every moment is precious. I can't imagine why his nieces keep putting it off. Perhaps God will help me find a way to prepare him! Goodbye, Prince! May God give you strength..."
[Speaking in French] "Goodbye, my dear," answered Prince Vasili, turning away from her.
"Oh, he's in a terrible state," said the mother to her son when they were in the carriage. "He barely recognizes anyone."
"I don't understand, Mama—what is his attitude toward Pierre?" asked the son.
"The will shall show, my dear. Our fate depends on it too."
"But why do you expect him to leave us anything?"
"Oh, my dear! He's so rich, and we're so poor!"
"Well, that's hardly a good enough reason, Mama..."
"Oh, God! How ill he is!" the mother cried.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After Anna Mikhaylovna had driven off with her son to visit Count Cyril Vladimirovich Bezukhov, Countess Rostova sat alone for a long time, pressing her handkerchief to her eyes. At last she rang the bell.
"What's the matter with you, my dear?" she said irritably to the maid who had kept her waiting several minutes. "Don't you want to serve me? Then I'll find you another position."

The countess was upset by her friend's sorrow and humiliating poverty, and was therefore in a bad mood—a state that, with her, always expressed itself in calling her maid "my dear" and speaking to her with exaggerated politeness.
"I'm very sorry, ma'am," the maid replied.
"Ask the count to come to me."
The count came waddling in to see his wife, looking somewhat guilty as usual.
"Well, little countess! What a game stew in Madeira sauce we're going to have, my dear! I tried it. The thousand rubles I paid for Taras were well spent. He's worth it!"
He sat down beside his wife, elbows on his knees, running his hands through his gray hair.
"What are your orders, little countess?"
"You see, my dear... What's that mess?" she said, pointing at his waistcoat. "It's the stew, most likely," she added with a smile. "Well, the thing is, Count, I need some money."
Her face turned sad.
"Oh, little countess!"... And the count began fumbling for his pocketbook.
"I need a lot, Count! I need five hundred rubles," and taking out her cambric handkerchief, she began wiping her husband's waistcoat.
"Yes, right away, right away! Hey, who's there?" he called out in a tone used only by people who are certain their summons will be instantly obeyed. "Send Dmitri to me!"
Dmitri, a man from a good family who had been raised in the count's household and now managed all his affairs, stepped quietly into the room.

"This is what I need, my dear fellow," said the count to the respectful young man. "Bring me..." He thought for a moment. "Yes, bring me seven hundred rubles. But make sure you don't bring me tattered, dirty notes like last time—nice clean ones, for the countess."
"Yes, Dmitri, clean ones, please," said the countess with a deep sigh.

"When would you like them, your excellency?" asked Dmitri. "If I may mention... But don't worry," he added quickly, noticing that the count was beginning to breathe hard and fast—always a sign that anger was approaching. "I forgot... Shall I bring them right away?"
"Yes, yes, just so! Bring it. Give it to the countess."
"What a treasure that Dmitri is," the count added with a smile when the young man had gone. "There's never any 'impossible' with him. That's a thing I can't stand! Everything is possible."
"Ah, money, Count, money! What sorrow it causes in this world," said the countess. "But I desperately need this sum."
"You, my little countess, are a well-known spendthrift," said the count, and having kissed his wife's hand, he went back to his study.

When Anna Mikhaylovna returned from Count Bezukhov's, the money—all in clean notes—was lying ready under a handkerchief on the countess's little table. Anna Mikhaylovna could see that something was troubling her friend.
"Well, my dear?" asked the countess.
"Oh, what a terrible state he's in! You wouldn't recognize him, he's so ill! I was only there a few minutes and barely said a word..."
"Annette, for heaven's sake, don't refuse me," the countess began, with a blush that looked very strange on her thin, dignified, elderly face, and she took the money from under the handkerchief.
Anna Mikhaylovna instantly guessed what she intended and bent forward, ready to embrace the countess at the right moment.
"This is for Boris, from me—for his outfit."

Anna Mikhaylovna was already embracing her and weeping. The countess wept too. They wept because they were friends, and because they were kind-hearted, and because they—friends since childhood—had to think about such a base thing as money, and because their youth was over. But those tears were pleasant to them both.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: Countess Rostova, with her daughters and a large number of guests, was already seated in the drawing room. The count had taken the gentlemen into his study to show them his prized collection of Turkish pipes. Every now and then he popped out to ask, "Hasn't she come yet?" They were expecting Marya Dmitrievna Akhrosimova, known in society as "the terrible dragon"—a lady distinguished not by wealth or rank but by common sense and blunt honesty. Marya Dmitrievna was known to the imperial family as well as to all of Moscow and Petersburg, and both cities marveled at her, privately laughed at her rudeness, and told amusing stories about her, while nonetheless everyone without exception respected and feared her.

In the count's study, which was thick with tobacco smoke, the men talked about the war that had just been announced in an imperial manifesto and about the military draft. None of them had actually seen the manifesto, but they all knew it had been issued. The count sat on the sofa between two smoking, chatting guests. He neither smoked nor talked himself but kept tilting his head from one side to the other, watching the smokers with obvious pleasure and listening to his two neighbors' conversation, which he kept stoking by setting them against each other.

One of them was a sallow, clean-shaven civilian with a thin, wrinkled face, already aging despite being dressed like the most fashionable young man. He sat with his legs up on the sofa as though completely at home and, having stuck an amber mouthpiece deep into his mouth, was inhaling the smoke in jerks and squinting. This was Shinshin, an old bachelor and cousin of the countess—a man with "a sharp tongue," as Moscow society put it. He seemed to be looking down on his companion. The other man, a fresh-faced, rosy Guards officer, immaculately washed, brushed, and buttoned, held his pipe in the center of his mouth and with red lips gently drew in the smoke, letting it escape from his handsome mouth in rings. This was Lieutenant Berg of the Semenov regiment, with whom Boris was to travel to join the army, and about whom Natasha had teased her older sister Vera, calling Berg her "intended." The count sat between them, listening attentively. His favorite pastime, when he wasn't playing boston—a card game he adored—was being an audience, especially when he managed to set two talkative people at each other.

[Speaking in French] "Well then, old boy, my most honorable Alphonse Karlovich," said Shinshin, laughing ironically and mixing the most common Russian expressions with the choicest French phrases—a quirk of his speech. "You plan to make your fortune off the government—you want to turn a profit from your company?"
* You expect to make an income out of the government.
"No, Pyotr Nikolaevich, I only want to point out that the advantages in the cavalry are far fewer than in the infantry. Just consider my own situation, Pyotr Nikolaevich..."

Berg always spoke quietly, politely, and with great precision. His conversation invariably revolved around himself; he could remain calm and silent when the talk had nothing to do with him. He could sit quiet for hours without the slightest discomfort to himself or anyone else, but the moment the conversation touched on him personally, he would begin speaking at length and with obvious satisfaction.

"Consider my position, Pyotr Nikolaevich. If I were in the cavalry, I'd receive no more than two hundred rubles every four months, even at the rank of lieutenant. But as it is, I receive two hundred and thirty," he said, looking at Shinshin and the count with a happy, pleasant smile, as though it were self-evident that his success must be everyone else's chief concern.

"On top of that, Pyotr Nikolaevich, by transferring to the Guards I'll be in a more prominent position," Berg continued, "and vacancies open up much more frequently in the Foot Guards. And just think what you can do with two hundred and thirty rubles! I even manage to save a little and send something to my father," he went on, blowing a smoke ring.
[Speaking in French] "That balances the books... A German can skin a flint, as the proverb goes," Shinshin remarked, shifting his pipe to the other side of his mouth and winking at the count.
* So that squares matters.

The count burst out laughing. Other guests, seeing that Shinshin was holding forth, came over to listen. Berg, oblivious to irony or indifference, went on explaining how by transferring to the Guards he had already gained an advantage over his old comrades from the Cadet Corps; how in wartime the company commander might be killed and he, as the most senior man in the company, could easily succeed to the post; how popular he was with everyone in the regiment; and how pleased his father was with him. Berg clearly enjoyed telling all this and apparently had no idea that other people might have their own interests. But everything he said was so neatly composed, and the naivety of his youthful self-absorption was so transparent, that he disarmed his listeners.
"Well, my boy, you'll get on wherever you go—infantry or cavalry—I'll vouch for that," said Shinshin, patting him on the shoulder and swinging his feet off the sofa.
Berg smiled with delight. The count, followed by his guests, moved into the drawing room.

It was that moment just before a grand dinner when the assembled guests, expecting the call to appetizers, avoid any lengthy conversation but feel compelled to move about and chat—to show they aren't the least bit impatient for their food. The host and hostess keep glancing toward the door and exchanging looks, and the visitors try to guess from these glances who or what is being waited for—some important relative who hasn't arrived yet, or a dish that isn't quite ready.
* Hors d'oeuvres.

Pierre had arrived just at dinnertime and was sitting awkwardly in the middle of the drawing room on the first chair he'd come across, blocking everyone's path. The countess tried to draw him into conversation, but he just kept looking around through his spectacles as if searching for someone and answered all her questions in monosyllables. He was in everyone's way and was the only person who didn't notice it. Most of the guests, who knew about the bear incident, studied this big, stout, quiet man with curiosity, wondering how such a clumsy, modest fellow could have pulled such a stunt on a policeman.
"You've only just arrived?" the countess asked him.
[Speaking in French] "Yes, madame," he replied, looking around.
"You haven't seen my husband yet?"
[Speaking in French] "No, madame." He smiled quite inappropriately.
"You've been in Paris recently, I believe? It must be very interesting."
"Very interesting."

The countess exchanged glances with Anna Mikhaylovna. Anna Mikhaylovna understood she was being asked to entertain this young man, and sitting down beside him she began talking about his father; but he answered her, as he had the countess, only in monosyllables. The other guests were all chattering among themselves. "The Razumovskys... It was charming... You are so kind... Countess Apraksina..." could be heard on all sides. The countess rose and went into the ballroom.
"Marya Dmitrievna?" her voice called from there.
"Herself," came the answer in a rough voice, and Marya Dmitrievna entered the room.

All the unmarried women and even the married ones—except the very oldest—stood up. Marya Dmitrievna paused in the doorway. Tall and stout, holding high her fifty-year-old head with its gray curls, she surveyed the guests and deliberately adjusted her wide sleeves as if rolling them up. Marya Dmitrievna always spoke in Russian.

"Health and happiness to the birthday girl and to her children," she said in her loud, full-bodied voice, which drowned out all others. "Well, you old sinner," she went on, turning to the count, who was kissing her hand, "feeling bored in Moscow, are you? Nowhere to hunt with your dogs? But what can you do, old man? Just look how these little ones are growing up!" And she pointed at the girls. "You'll have to find husbands for them whether you like it or not..."

"Well," she said, "how's my Cossack?" (Marya Dmitrievna always called Natasha a Cossack.) She stroked the child's arm as Natasha came up fearlessly and cheerfully to kiss her hand. "I know she's a little terror, but I like her."

She pulled a pair of pear-shaped ruby earrings from her enormous handbag and, having given them to the glowing Natasha, who was beaming with the joy of her name-day celebration, turned away at once and addressed Pierre.

"Hey, hey, friend! Come here," she said, dropping her voice to a soft, high tone. "Come here, my friend..." And she ominously rolled up her sleeves even higher. Pierre approached, looking at her with childlike trust through his spectacles.

"Come closer, come closer, friend! I used to be the only person who told your father the truth when he was in favor, and in your case it's clearly my duty too." She paused. Everyone went silent, sensing that what had come so far was merely the introduction.
"A fine lad! Oh, a fine lad! His father lies on his deathbed and he amuses himself strapping a policeman to a bear! For shame, sir, for shame! You'd be better off going to the war."
She turned away and gave her hand to the count, who was struggling not to laugh.
"Well, I think it's time for dinner, isn't it?" said Marya Dmitrievna.

The count went in first with Marya Dmitrievna; the countess followed on the arm of a colonel of hussars—a man of great importance to them because Nicholas was going to join his regiment. Then came Anna Mikhaylovna with Shinshin. Berg offered his arm to Vera. The smiling Julie Karagina went in with Nicholas. After them more couples followed, filling the entire dining hall, and last of all came the children, tutors, and governesses, one by one. The footmen began bustling about, chairs scraped, the band struck up in the gallery, and the guests took their seats. Then the music of the count's household band gave way to the clatter of knives and forks, the hum of voices, and the soft steps of the servants. At one end of the table sat the countess with Marya Dmitrievna on her right and Anna Mikhaylovna on her left, with the other lady guests farther down. At the other end sat the count, with the hussar colonel on his left and Shinshin and the other men on his right. Halfway down the long table on one side sat the young people: Vera next to Berg, and Pierre next to Boris; on the other side sat the children, tutors, and governesses. From behind the crystal decanters and fruit bowls, the count kept glancing at his wife and her tall cap with its light-blue ribbons, and busily filled his neighbors' glasses without neglecting his own. The countess, for her part, never forgetting her duties as hostess, threw pointed glances from behind the pineapples at her husband, whose red face and bald head seemed to stand out even more than usual against his gray hair. At the ladies' end a steady hum of conversation never let up; at the men's end the voices grew louder and louder, especially that of the hussar colonel, who ate and drank so much that his face grew increasingly flushed, and the count held him up as an example to the other guests. Berg, with tender smiles, was telling Vera that love is not an earthly but a heavenly feeling. Boris was pointing out the various guests to his new friend Pierre and exchanging glances with Natasha, who sat across from him. Pierre said little but studied the new faces and ate a great deal. Of the two soups he chose turtle with savory pastries and went on to the game course without skipping a single dish or any of the wines. These the butler offered slyly from behind the next man's shoulder, bottle wrapped in a napkin, whispering: "Dry Madeira"... "Hungarian"... or "Rhine wine" as the case might be. Of the four crystal glasses engraved with the count's monogram that stood before his place, Pierre held out whichever one came to hand and drank with pleasure, gazing at the other guests with ever-growing warmth. Natasha, who sat across from him, was looking at Boris the way thirteen-year-old girls look at a boy they're in love with and have just kissed for the first time. Sometimes that same look fell on Pierre, and that funny, lively little girl's gaze made him want to laugh without knowing why.

Nicholas sat some distance from Sonya, beside Julie Karagina, chatting with her with the same involuntary smile. Sonya wore a polite social smile but was obviously tortured by jealousy; first she turned pale, then blushed, straining every nerve to overhear what Nicholas and Julie were saying to each other. The governess kept glancing around anxiously, as if ready to defend against any slight to the children. The German tutor was trying to memorize all the dishes, wines, and desserts so he could send a full description of the dinner to his family in Germany; he was deeply offended when the butler carrying a napkin-wrapped bottle passed right by him. He frowned, trying to look as if he didn't want any of that wine, but he was mortified—because no one seemed to understand that it wasn't thirst or greed that made him want it, but simply a conscientious desire for knowledge.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: The card tables were brought out, groups formed for boston, and the count's visitors settled themselves—some in the two drawing rooms, some in the sitting room, some in the library.

The count, holding his cards spread out like a fan, struggled to stay awake after dinner and laughed at everything. The young people, at the countess's suggestion, gathered around the clavichord and harp. Julie was asked to play first, by general request. After she performed a little air with variations on the harp, she joined the other young women in begging Natasha and Nicholas—who were known for their musical talent—to sing something. Natasha, who was being treated as though she were already grown up, was clearly very proud of this but also felt shy.
"What should we sing?" she asked.
"'The Brook,'" Nicholas suggested.
"All right, let's hurry. Boris, come here," said Natasha. "But where's Sonya?"
She looked around and, not seeing her friend in the room, ran off to find her.

Running into Sonya's room and not finding her there, Natasha ran to the nursery—but Sonya wasn't there either. Natasha guessed she must be on the chest in the hallway. The chest in the hallway was the traditional place of mourning for the younger girls in the Rostov household. And sure enough, there was Sonya, lying face down on the nurse's dirty feather bed on top of the chest, crumpling her gauzy pink dress beneath her, hiding her face in her slender fingers, and sobbing so hard that her bare little shoulders shook. Natasha's face—which had been so radiantly happy all through this name-day celebration—suddenly changed: her eyes went blank, then a shiver ran down her broad neck and the corners of her mouth drooped.

"Sonya! What is it? What's the matter?... Oh... Oh... Oh!" And Natasha's wide mouth stretched open, making her look almost ugly, and she began to wail like a baby for no reason other than that Sonya was crying. Sonya tried to lift her head to answer but couldn't, and buried her face deeper in the bed. Natasha wept, sitting on the blue-striped feather bed and hugging her friend. With an effort Sonya sat up and began wiping her eyes and trying to explain.

"Nicholas is going away in a week, his... papers... have come... he told me himself... but still I shouldn't cry," and she showed a sheet of paper she was holding—the verses Nicholas had written—"still, I shouldn't cry, but you can't... no one can understand... what a soul he has!"
And she started crying again because he had such a noble soul.

"It's easy for you... I'm not jealous... I love you and Boris too," she went on, gaining a little strength. "He's nice... there are no obstacles in your way... But Nicholas is my cousin... one would have to... the Metropolitan himself... and even then it can't be done. And besides, if she tells Mama"—Sonya considered the countess her mother and called her that—"that I'm ruining Nicholas's career and that I'm heartless and ungrateful, when truly... God is my witness"—she crossed herself—"I love her so much, and all of you, only Vera... And what for? What have I done to her? I'm so grateful to you that I'd willingly sacrifice everything, only I have nothing..."
Sonya couldn't go on and hid her face again in her hands and in the feather bed. Natasha tried to comfort her, but her face showed she understood the full weight of her friend's trouble.
"Sonya," she burst out suddenly, as if she'd guessed the real reason for her friend's grief, "I'm sure Vera said something to you after dinner. Didn't she?"

"Yes—these are the verses Nicholas wrote himself, and I copied some others, and she found them on my table and said she'd show them to Mama. She said I was ungrateful, and that Mama would never let him marry me, and that he'd marry Julie. You saw how he's been with her all day... Natasha, what have I done to deserve this?"
And she began to sob again, more bitterly than before. Natasha pulled her up, hugged her, and, smiling through her own tears, started to comfort her.

"Sonya, don't believe her, darling! Don't believe her! Remember how we all talked—you and Nicholas and me—in the sitting room after supper? We worked out how everything would be arranged. I don't remember exactly how, but don't you remember that it could all work out and how wonderful it would be? There's Uncle Shinshin's brother who married his first cousin. And we're only second cousins, you know. And Boris says it's perfectly possible. You know I've told him all about it. And he's so clever and so good!" said Natasha. "Don't cry, Sonya, dear love, darling Sonya!" And she kissed her and laughed. "Vera is spiteful—never mind her! Everything will be all right, and she won't say anything to Mama. Nicholas will tell her himself, and he doesn't care about Julie at all."
Natasha kissed her on the hair.
Sonya sat up. The little kitten brightened, its eyes shone, and it seemed ready to raise its tail, hop down on its soft paws, and start playing with a ball of yarn the way a kitten should.
"Do you think so?... Really? Truly?" she asked, quickly smoothing her dress and hair.
"Really, truly!" Natasha answered, tucking a wayward curl back under her friend's braid.
Both girls laughed.
"Well, let's go sing 'The Brook.'"
"Let's go!"
"You know, that fat Pierre who sat across from me is so funny!" said Natasha, stopping suddenly. "I feel so happy!"
And she took off running down the hallway.

Sonya, brushing off bits of down that clung to her and tucking the verses into the front of her dress against her thin little chest, ran after Natasha down the hallway into the sitting room, her face flushed, her steps light and joyful. At the guests' request the young people sang the quartet "The Brook," which delighted everyone. Then Nicholas sang a song he had just learned:
In the moonlight's gentle glow, How sweet, as fancies wander free, To know that in this world below There's one who's thinking still of thee!
That as her fingers touch the harp, Sending sweet music o'er the lea, It is for thee her heart beats sharp, Breathing its message out to thee...
A day or two, then joy unspoiled— But oh, till then I cannot live!...
He hadn't finished the last verse before the young people began getting ready to dance in the great hall, and the sound of feet and musicians coughing drifted down from the gallery.

Pierre was sitting in the drawing room where Shinshin had drawn him into a political conversation—as someone recently returned from abroad—in which several others had joined but which bored Pierre. When the music started, Natasha came in and walked straight up to Pierre, laughing and blushing.
"Mama told me to ask you to join the dancing."
"I'm afraid I'll mix up the figures," Pierre replied, "but if you'll be my teacher..." And lowering his big arm, he offered it to the slender little girl.

While the couples were arranging themselves and the musicians tuning up, Pierre sat down with his small partner. Natasha was perfectly happy—she was dancing with a grown-up man who had been abroad. She was sitting in a prominent spot, talking to him like a proper lady. She had a fan in her hand that one of the women had given her to hold. Striking quite the pose of a society woman—heaven knows when or where she'd learned it—she chatted with her partner, fanning herself and smiling over the fan.
"Dear, dear! Just look at her!" exclaimed the countess as she crossed the ballroom, pointing at Natasha.
Natasha blushed and laughed.
"Well, really, Mama! Why not? What's so surprising?"

In the middle of the third ecossaise there was a clatter of chairs being pushed back in the sitting room, where the count and Marya Dmitrievna had been playing cards with most of the older, more distinguished guests. Now they stood up, stretching after sitting so long, put away their purses and wallets, and came into the ballroom. First came Marya Dmitrievna and the count, both looking very pleased with themselves. The count, with a playful ceremony that was almost balletic, offered his bent arm to Marya Dmitrievna. He drew himself up, a smile of debonair gallantry lit up his face, and as soon as the last figure of the ecossaise ended, he clapped his hands at the musicians and called up to their gallery, addressing the first violin:
"Semen! Do you know the Daniel Cooper?"
This was the count's favorite dance, one he had danced in his youth. (Strictly speaking, the Daniel Cooper was a single figure of the anglaise.)
"Look at Papa!" Natasha shouted to the whole room, and completely forgetting that she was dancing with a grown-up partner, she bent her curly head to her knees and filled the room with her laughter.

And indeed everyone in the room watched with amused delight as the jolly old gentleman took his place beside his tall, stout partner Marya Dmitrievna—curved his arms, beat time, straightened his shoulders, turned out his toes, tapped his foot lightly, and with a smile that kept spreading across his round face, prepared the audience for what was coming. The moment the provocatively cheerful strains of the Daniel Cooper began—a tune that sounded rather like a merry peasant dance—every doorway of the ballroom was suddenly filled with household servants, the men on one side and the women on the other, who had come with beaming faces to watch their master enjoy himself.
"Just look at the master! A real eagle!" the nurse declared loudly from one of the doorways.

The count danced well and knew it. But his partner could not dance well and had no desire to. Her enormous figure stood rigid, her powerful arms hanging at her sides (she had given her handbag to the countess), and only her stern but handsome face truly joined in the dance. Everything that the count's plump body expressed through movement, Marya Dmitrievna conveyed solely through her increasingly radiant face and quivering nose. But if the count charmed the spectators with the surprise of his nimble footwork and the agility with which he sprang about on his light feet, Marya Dmitrievna made no less of an impression through the slightest effort—a small shift of her shoulders, a bend of her arms while turning, a stamp of her foot—all of which everyone appreciated given her size and usual severity. The dance grew livelier and livelier. The other couples couldn't draw a moment's attention to themselves and didn't even try. Everyone was watching the count and Marya Dmitrievna. Natasha kept tugging at everyone's sleeves and dresses, urging them to "look at Papa!"—though they were already unable to tear their eyes away. In the pauses between steps the count, breathing hard, waved at the musicians and shouted for them to play faster. Faster, faster, and faster—more lightly, still more lightly—the count whirled around Marya Dmitrievna, now on his toes, now on his heels, until, spinning his partner back to her seat, he executed the final step, kicking his soft foot up behind him, bowing his sweating head, smiling, and sweeping his arm wide—to a thunder of applause and laughter, led by Natasha. Both dancers stood still, breathing heavily and mopping their faces with their handkerchiefs.
[Speaking in French] "That's how we used to dance in our day, my dear," said the count.
"Now that was a Daniel Cooper!" exclaimed Marya Dmitrievna, rolling up her sleeves and puffing hard.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: While the sixth anglaise was being danced at the Rostovs' ball, with the exhausted musicians stumbling through the tune and the tired footmen and cooks preparing supper, Count Bezukhov suffered his sixth stroke. The doctors declared there was no hope of recovery. After a silent confession, the dying man received communion, and preparations began for the sacrament of last rites. The house was filled with the nervous energy that always accompanies such moments. Outside the gates, a group of undertakers lurked in the shadows, hiding whenever a carriage pulled up, waiting for the lucrative order for an expensive funeral. The Military Governor of Moscow, who had been diligently sending aides to check on the count's condition, came in person that evening to pay his final respects to this celebrated nobleman from Catherine the Great's court, Count Bezukhov.

The grand reception room was packed. Everyone rose respectfully as the Military Governor emerged after spending about half an hour alone with the dying man. He gave a slight nod to acknowledge their bows and tried to get out as quickly as possible, avoiding the stares of the doctors, clergy, and family members. Prince Vasili, who had grown thinner and paler over the past few days, walked him to the door, repeating something to him several times in a low voice.

After the Military Governor left, Prince Vasili sat alone on a chair in the ballroom, crossing one leg high over the other, resting his elbow on his knee, and covering his face with his hand. He sat like that for a while, then stood up and, looking around with frightened eyes, hurried with unusually quick steps down the long corridor that led to the back of the house, toward the eldest princess's room.

The people in the dimly lit reception room spoke in nervous whispers, and whenever anyone entered or left the dying man's room, they fell silent and watched the door—which gave a slight creak when opened—with eyes full of curiosity or anticipation.
"The limits of human life are fixed and cannot be exceeded," an old priest was telling a lady who had sat down beside him and was listening with naive attention.
"I wonder if it's too late to administer last rites?" the lady asked, adding the priest's proper title, as though she had no opinion of her own on the matter.
"Ah, madam, it is a great sacrament," the priest replied, running his hand over the thin gray strands of hair combed across his bald head.
"Who was that? The Military Governor himself?" people were asking on the other side of the room. "How young he looks!"
"Yes, and he's over sixty. I hear the count no longer recognizes anyone. They wanted to administer last rites."
"I knew someone who received that sacrament seven times."

The second princess had just come from the sickroom with red, tear-swollen eyes and sat down next to Dr. Lorrain, who was seated in an elegant pose beneath a portrait of Catherine the Great, leaning his elbow on a table.
"Beautiful," the doctor said in response to a comment about the weather. "The weather is beautiful, Princess. And besides, in Moscow one feels almost as if one were in the country."
"Yes, indeed," the princess replied with a sigh. "So he may have something to drink?"
Lorrain considered this.
"Has he taken his medicine?"
"Yes."
The doctor glanced at his watch.
"Take a glass of boiled water and add a pinch of cream of tartar," he said, indicating with his delicate fingers what he meant by a pinch.
"There has never been a case," a German doctor was saying to an aide-de-camp, "where anyone survives the third stroke."
"And what a healthy man he was!" the aide-de-camp remarked. "And who will inherit his wealth?" he added in a whisper.
"It won't go begging," the German replied with a smile.
Everyone looked toward the door again as it creaked open and the second princess went in with the drink she had prepared according to Lorrain's instructions. The German doctor approached Lorrain.
[Speaking in French] "Do you think he can last until morning?" the German asked, addressing Lorrain in poorly pronounced French.
Lorrain pursed his lips and waved a firmly negative finger in front of his nose.
"Tonight, no later," he said quietly, then moved away with a composed smile of satisfaction at having been able to clearly assess and state the patient's condition.
Meanwhile, Prince Vasili had opened the door to the princess's room.

The room was almost dark, lit only by two small lamps burning before the icons, and filled with a pleasant scent of flowers and incense. It was crowded with small pieces of furniture—whatnots, cupboards, and little tables. Behind a screen, the white quilt of a high feather bed was just visible. A small dog began to bark.
"Ah, is that you, cousin?"
She rose and smoothed her hair, which was, as always, so impossibly smooth that it looked as though it were made of one piece with her head and coated in varnish.
"Has something happened?" she asked. "I'm so frightened."

"No, nothing has changed. I just came to talk business, Catiche," the prince muttered wearily, sinking into the chair she had just vacated. "You've certainly made it warm in here, I'll say that. Well, sit down. Let's talk."
*Catherine.
"I thought something might have happened," she said, her face set in its usual expression of stony severity. She sat down across from the prince and prepared to listen.
"I was trying to get some sleep, my dear cousin, but I can't."
"Well, my dear?" said Prince Vasili, taking her hand and bending it downward, as was his habit.
It was clear that this "well?" referred to much that they both understood without having to say it.

The princess, whose body was straight and rigid, disproportionately long for her legs, looked directly at Prince Vasili with no trace of emotion in her prominent gray eyes. Then she shook her head and glanced up at the icons with a sigh. This could have been taken as an expression of sorrow and devotion, or of weariness and a wish to rest soon. Prince Vasili took it as weariness.
"And what about me?" he said. "Do you think this is any easier for me? I'm worn out like a post horse, but I still need to talk with you, Catiche. A very serious talk."

Prince Vasili fell silent, and his cheeks began to twitch nervously—first one side, then the other—giving his face an unpleasant expression that would never have appeared in a drawing room. His eyes, too, seemed strange: at one moment they looked brazenly cunning, and at the next they darted around in alarm.

The princess, holding her little dog on her lap with her thin, bony hands, stared attentively into Prince Vasili's eyes, clearly resolved not to be the first to break the silence, even if she had to wait until morning.

"Well, you see, my dear princess and cousin, Catherine Semenovna," Prince Vasili continued, returning to his subject with what seemed like an inner struggle, "at a moment like this, one must think of everything. One must think of the future, of all of you... I love you all like my own children, as you know."
The princess continued to look at him without moving, her expression unchanged.

"And then, of course, my own family must also be considered," Prince Vasili went on, testily pushing a small table aside without looking at her. "You know, Catiche, that we—you three sisters, Mamontov, and my wife—are the count's only direct heirs. I know how difficult it is for you to talk or think about such things. It's no easier for me. But, my dear, I'm getting on toward sixty and must be prepared for anything. Did you know I've sent for Pierre? The count"—he pointed to the portrait on the wall—"specifically asked that he be called."
Prince Vasili looked questioningly at the princess, but couldn't tell whether she was weighing what he had said or simply staring at him.
"There is one thing I constantly pray God to grant, my dear cousin," she replied, "and that is that He would be merciful to him and allow his noble soul to peacefully depart this—"

"Yes, yes, of course," Prince Vasili interrupted impatiently, rubbing his bald head and angrily pulling back the little table he had just pushed away. "But... in short, the fact is... you know yourself that last winter the count made a will leaving all his property not to us, his direct heirs, but to Pierre."
"He's made plenty of wills!" the princess remarked quietly. "But he can't leave the estate to Pierre. Pierre is illegitimate."

"But my dear," said Prince Vasili suddenly, gripping the little table and becoming more animated, speaking more rapidly, "what if a letter has been written to the Emperor asking for Pierre's legitimation? You must understand that given the count's services, such a request would certainly be granted..."
The princess smiled the way people do when they think they know more about the subject than the person they're talking to.

"I can tell you even more," Prince Vasili continued, seizing her hand. "That letter was written, though never sent, and the Emperor knew about it. The only question is whether it has been destroyed. If it hasn't, then as soon as it's all over"—Prince Vasili sighed to make clear what he meant by 'all over'—"and the count's papers are opened, the will and the letter will be delivered to the Emperor, and the petition will certainly be granted. Pierre will get everything as the legitimate son."
"And what about our share?" asked the princess with an ironic smile, as though anything might happen except that.

"But my poor Catiche, it's as clear as daylight! He'll be the legal heir to everything, and you won't get a thing. You must know, my dear, whether the will and letter were written and whether they've been destroyed. And if by some chance they've been overlooked, you need to know where they are, and you must find them, because..."

"What next?" the princess interrupted with a sardonic smile, her eyes unchanged. "I am a woman, and you think we're all stupid. But I know this: an illegitimate son cannot inherit... [Speaking in French] a bastard!" she added, as though this French translation would conclusively prove the invalidity of his argument.
* A bastard.

"Really, Catiche! Can't you understand? You're so intelligent—how can you not see that if the count has written to the Emperor asking him to recognize Pierre as legitimate, then Pierre will no longer be plain Pierre but Count Bezukhov, and he'll inherit everything under the will? And if the will and letter haven't been destroyed, you'll have nothing but the consolation of having been dutiful, [Speaking in French] and all that follows from that! That's certain."
* And all that follows therefrom.

"I know the will was made, but I also know it's invalid. And you, my dear cousin, seem to take me for a complete fool," said the princess with the expression women wear when they think they're being witty and cutting.

"My dear Princess Catherine Semenovna," Prince Vasili began impatiently, "I didn't come here to argue with you, but to discuss your interests as a kinsman—a good, kind, loyal relative. I'm telling you for the tenth time: if the letter to the Emperor and the will in Pierre's favor are among the count's papers, then, my dear girl, you and your sisters are not heirs! If you don't believe me, believe the experts. I've just spoken with Dmitri Onufrich"—the family lawyer—"and he says the same thing."

At this, something suddenly shifted in the princess's manner. Her thin lips went white, though her eyes remained unchanged, and when she spoke, her voice passed through such transitions that she herself was clearly surprised by them.
"That would be wonderful!" she said. "I never wanted anything, and I don't now."
She pushed the little dog off her lap and straightened her dress.
"And this is the gratitude—this is the recognition for those who sacrificed everything for him!" she cried. "Splendid! Just fine! I don't want anything, Prince."
"Yes, but you're not the only one. There are your sisters..." Prince Vasili replied.
But the princess wasn't listening.
"Yes, I knew it long ago but had forgotten. I knew I could expect nothing but meanness, deceit, envy, and intrigue in this house—the blackest ingratitude..."
"Do you or do you not know where that will is?" Prince Vasili insisted, his cheeks twitching more violently than ever.
"Yes, I was a fool! I still believed in people, loved them, sacrificed myself for them. But only the base and the vile succeed! I know who's been scheming!"
The princess tried to stand, but the prince held her by the hand. She looked like someone who had suddenly lost all faith in the human race. She shot her companion an angry glance.

"There's still time, my dear. You must remember, Catiche, that it was all done hastily, in a moment of anger and illness, and was forgotten afterward. Our duty, my dear, is to correct his mistake—to ease his last moments by preventing this injustice, and not to let him die feeling he has made miserable those who..."

"Who sacrificed everything for him," the princess chimed in, and she would have stood again if the prince hadn't still been holding her. "Though he never knew how to appreciate it. No, my dear cousin," she added with a sigh, "I shall always remember that in this world one must expect no reward—that in this world there is neither honor nor justice. In this world one has to be cunning and cruel."
"Now, now! Be reasonable. I know your excellent heart."
"No, I have a wicked heart."

"I know your heart," the prince repeated. "I value your friendship and want you to think well of me. Don't upset yourself, and let us talk sensibly while there's still time—whether it's a day or only an hour. Tell me everything you know about the will, and above all, where it is. You must know. We'll take it to the count immediately. No doubt he's forgotten all about it and will want to destroy it. You understand that my only desire is to faithfully carry out his wishes—that's my sole reason for being here. I came simply to help him and you."
"Now I see it all! I know who's been scheming—I know!" the princess cried.
"That's not the point, my dear."
"It's that protégée of yours, that sweet Princess Drubetskaya, that Anna Mikhaylovna whom I wouldn't hire as a housemaid... the infamous, vile woman!"
"Let's not waste any time..."

"Oh, don't talk to me about it! Last winter she wormed her way in here and told the count such vile, disgraceful things about us—especially about Sophie—I can't even repeat them. It made the count so ill that he refused to see us for two whole weeks. I know that was when he wrote that vile, infamous document, but I thought it was invalid."
"So we've finally gotten to it—why didn't you tell me about this sooner?"

"It's in the inlaid portfolio he keeps under his pillow," said the princess, ignoring his question. "Now I know! Yes—if I have a sin, a great sin, it is hatred of that vile woman!" she nearly shrieked, now completely transformed. "And what is she doing here, worming her way in? But I'll give her a piece of my mind. The time will come!"

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: While these conversations were taking place in the reception room and the princess's room, a carriage carrying Pierre—who had been sent for—and Anna Mikhaylovna, who felt it necessary to accompany him, was pulling into the courtyard of Count Bezukhov's house. As the wheels rolled softly over the straw that had been laid beneath the windows, Anna Mikhaylovna turned to offer some comforting words to her companion—and realized he was asleep in his corner. She woke him up. Pierre roused himself and followed Anna Mikhaylovna out of the carriage, only then beginning to think about the visit with his dying father that lay ahead. He noticed they hadn't come to the front entrance but to a back door. As he was climbing down from the carriage, two men who looked like tradesmen darted away from the entrance and hid in the shadows along the wall. Pausing, Pierre spotted several other men of the same type lurking in the shadows on both sides of the house. But neither Anna Mikhaylovna nor the footman nor the coachman—who couldn't have missed seeing them—paid any attention. "It must be all right," Pierre told himself, and followed Anna Mikhaylovna. She hurried up a narrow, dimly lit stone staircase, calling back to Pierre, who was falling behind, to keep up. Though he couldn't see why it was necessary for him to visit the count at all, much less why they had to use the back stairs, Anna Mikhaylovna's air of confidence and urgency made Pierre conclude that it was all absolutely essential. Halfway up, they were nearly knocked over by some men carrying pails who came clattering down the stairs in heavy boots. These men pressed themselves against the wall to let Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna pass, showing not the slightest surprise at seeing them there.
"Is this the way to the princesses' apartments?" Anna Mikhaylovna asked one of them.
"Yes," a footman answered in a bold, loud voice, as though anything were now permissible. "The door on the left, ma'am."
"Perhaps the count didn't ask for me," Pierre said when they reached the landing. "I'd better go to my own room."
Anna Mikhaylovna stopped and waited for him to catch up.
"Oh, my friend!" she said, touching his arm just as she had touched her son's that afternoon. "Believe me, I'm suffering no less than you are, but be a man!"
"But really, shouldn't I just go?" he asked, looking at her kindly over his spectacles.

"Oh, my dear friend! Forget whatever wrongs may have been done to you. Remember—he is your father... perhaps in the agony of death." She sighed. "I've loved you like a son from the very beginning. Trust me, Pierre. I won't forget your interests."
Pierre didn't understand a word of this, but his growing conviction that all of it was necessary only strengthened, and he meekly followed Anna Mikhaylovna, who was already opening a door.

The door led into a back anteroom. In one corner, an old servant of the princesses sat knitting a stocking. Pierre had never been in this part of the house and didn't even know these rooms existed. Anna Mikhaylovna addressed a maid hurrying past with a decanter on a tray as "my dear" and "my sweet," asked about the princess's health, and then led Pierre down a stone passage. The first door on the left opened into the princesses' apartments. The maid with the decanter, in her haste, had left the door open—everything in the house was being done in haste just then—and as Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna passed, they instinctively glanced inside.
